newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - March 13.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - March 13.

text.p: The New York Times reported the following business stories on Thursday:
* Staples and Office Depot agreed to sell 63 stores to their lone rival, OfficeMax Inc, to appease Federal antitrust regulators who are threatening to block their merger.
* Marsh & McLennan Cos and Johnson & Higgins agreed to merge in an $1.8 billion deal to create the world's largest insurance broker.

* Dow Jones & Co made the first change in its industrial average in nearly six years, replacing Bethlehem Steel, Texaco, Westinghouse and Woolworth Corp with Hewlett-Packard, Johnson & Johnson, the Travelers Group and Wal-Mart.
* The nation's real estate developers have begun building again after the end of the 1980s rush, but this time they are creating smaller offices in the suburbs rather than downtown skyscrapers.
* The Federal Reserve's latest survey of economic indicators suggests that American workers have been unable to win significantly higher pay despite low unemployment.
* BankAmerica named Eugene Lockhart Jr, the chief executive of Mastercard International, as president of its consumer banking division.
* General Electric Chairman and Chief Executive John Welch earned $6.3 million in salary and bonus last year, an 18.4 percent increase over his 1995 compensation.
* Sylvan Learning Systems agreed to buy National Education Corp for about $750 million in stock.
* Toys R Us said earnings rose nearly fourfold after charges, while Woolworth reported a fourth quarter profit compared with a year-ago loss.
* General Mills said fiscal third quarter earnings rose 5.6 percent, despite drops in sales and domestic cereal volume.

* Regulators fined Smith Barney and Lehman Bros $250,000 each and ordered the companies to pay a combined total of more than $5.6 million in refunds to customers who were overcharged when they sold mutual funds.

* General Motors released a financial breakdown of its operations, confirming analysts' beliefs that profits from its Delphi Automotive Systems auto parts unit have been supporting weak results in its car-making business.
* A new study to be published on Thursday shows for-profit hospitals spend at least 23 percent more on administrative costs than public or not-for-profit hospitals.

* A group of members of Congress gave 15 examples of tax breaks and government programs that they call corporate welfare, including benefits for insurance companies, firms doing business overseas and entertainment expenses.
* Analysis: Rupert Murdoch's plans to invest $1 billion in a satellite television service to be called Sky have made him an ominous figure to both the cable and broadcasting industries.
